summary: Jesus warns of coming persecution, promises that the Helper will come when He goes, and tells His grieving disciples that their sorrow will turn to joy.
key_insight: Earlier that evening Peter and Thomas had both asked where Jesus was going (13:36; 14:5). Now He says, “none of you asks Me, ‘Where are You going?’” They had asked about losing Him, not about where He was going and what it would bring them. Sorrow had filled their hearts, so they could not yet see the gain: “It is to your advantage that I go away.”
story: “These things I have spoken to you, that you should not be made to stumble.” They would be put out of the synagogues, and the time was coming when whoever killed them would think he was offering God service. People would do this because they had not known the Father or Him. He had not told them this at the beginning, because He was with them.

Now He was going away to the One who sent Him, and sorrow had filled their hearts. “Nevertheless I tell you the truth. It is to your advantage that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you; but if I depart, I will send Him to you.” When the Helper came, He would convict the world of sin, because they did not believe in Jesus; of righteousness, because Jesus was going to the Father; and of judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged.

He had many more things to tell them, but they could not bear them yet. “However, when He, the Spirit of truth, has come, He will guide you into all truth.” The Spirit would not speak on His own authority but would speak what He heard and tell them things to come. “He will glorify Me, for He will take of what is Mine and declare it to you.”

“A little while, and you will not see Me; and again a little while, and you will see Me.” The disciples puzzled over this among themselves: “We do not know what He is saying.” Jesus knew they wanted to ask Him. They would weep and lament while the world rejoiced, “but your sorrow will be turned into joy.” A woman in labor has sorrow because her hour has come, but when the child is born she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy. “Therefore you now have sorrow; but I will see you again and your heart will rejoice, and your joy no one will take from you.”

In that day they would ask the Father in His name, and He would give it to them. “Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full.” The Father Himself loved them, because they had loved Jesus and believed that He came from God. “I came forth from the Father and have come into the world. Again, I leave the world and go to the Father.”

His disciples said, “See, now You are speaking plainly,” and they declared, “By this we believe that You came forth from God.” Jesus answered, “Do you now believe?” The hour had come when they would be scattered, each to his own, and leave Him alone. “And yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me. These things I have spoken to you, that in Me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation; but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world.”

scene.label: The Helper
scene.text: The Greek word paraklētos means one called to stand alongside: a helper, an advocate. John uses the same word for Jesus in his first letter: “we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). That is why Jesus calls the Spirit “another Helper” (14:16), one who will be to them what He has been.

scene.label: Put out of the synagogue
scene.text: Expulsion from the synagogue cut a Jew off from worship, community and often a living. John has already shown it happen to the man born blind (9:22, 34) and noted rulers who hid their faith for fear of it (12:42). Saul of Tarsus would later persecute believers, convinced he was serving God (Acts 26:9–11).

scene.label: A woman in labor
scene.text: The prophets used the pains of childbirth for the anguish that comes just before God’s deliverance (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–9). The pain is real and it comes first, but it gives way to new life.

scene.label: “A little while”
scene.text: Within a day Jesus would be dead and buried, and on the third day they would see Him again. Many also hear in His words the longer “little while” until His return. Both fit His promise that their joy would not be taken away.

witnesses.john: Only John records this part of the farewell. It completes Jesus’ teaching on the Spirit, who will convict the world and guide the apostles into all truth; John’s own Gospel is part of that promised remembering and guiding (14:26; 16:13). The discourse ends not with the disciples’ confidence, which Jesus questions, but with His: “I have overcome the world.”

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks as the Victor on the eve of His death. He foresees the scattering of His followers, His own aloneness and the world’s hatred, and still says, “I have overcome the world.” He sends His people the Spirit, who makes Him known and brings Him glory.
seeing.living: Jesus does not promise His followers an easy road; He promises tribulation and peace together. When sorrow fills your heart, take His word that it is labor, not loss, and ask the Father in His name. Rely on the Spirit of truth to keep pointing you back to Jesus.
seeing.ponder: What sorrow are you carrying that Jesus may be turning into a joy no one can take from you?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus’ going brings the Spirit, and His victory turns His people’s sorrow into joy.
preaching.watch_for: Jesus repeats “These things I have spoken to you” through the farewell (14:25; 15:11; 16:1, 25, 33), often naming His purpose: that their joy may be full (15:11), that they would not stumble (16:1), and finally that in Him they may have peace (16:33). The discourse that began with troubled hearts (14:1) ends with peace and good cheer.
